text: Intelligence is not a gift, it's a privilege. You use it for the good of mankind.
claimed_attribution: Dr. Otto Octavius (Alfred Molina) — frequently misattributed online to the Ancient One in Doctor Strange
verified_attribution: Dr. Otto Octavius — Spider-Man 2 (2004), spoken to Peter Parker before the fusion reactor demonstration

source.locator: Octavius's apartment/lab scene, before the fusion experiment

context: Delivered as Octavius's stated ethos moments before hubris runs the experiment anyway — the line lands because he fails his own test.

text: Elementary, my dear Watson.
claimed_attribution: Sherlock Holmes — Arthur Conan Doyle stories
verified_attribution: Never appears verbatim in the Doyle canon; closest is 'Elementary,' said he, in 'The Adventure of the Crooked Man' (1893), with 'my dear Watson' used separately elsewhere. An early exact phrasing appears in P. G. Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist (1915).

source.locator: Doyle canon: 'The Crooked Man' (1893); Wodehouse: Psmith, Journalist (1915)

context: The most famous line in detective fiction was never written by its author — the canonical example of a quotation becoming true through repetition.

receipts.ref: Conan Doyle, 'The Adventure of the Crooked Man' (1893)

text: Be the change you wish to see in the world.
verified_attribution: No documented instance in Gandhi's writings or speeches; closest verified passage is a 1913 Indian Opinion article: 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change.'

source.locator: Gandhi's 'Snake' article passage, per Quote Investigator

context: The aphorism is a faithful compression of Gandhi's position but not his words — a paraphrase that ate its source.

text: Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.
verified_attribution: Earliest documented appearance is a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet: 'Insanity is repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results.' No Einstein connection has ever been found.

source.locator: per Quote Investigator, earliest known print citation

context: Assigned to Einstein by repetition — the aphorism's real lesson is about the attribution system, not the physics.

text: With great power there must also come — great responsibility!
claimed_attribution: Uncle Ben, as spoken advice to Peter Parker
verified_attribution: Stan Lee's narration caption, Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) — the line appears as a closing narrator caption, not as dialogue from Uncle Ben; later film adaptations moved it into Ben's mouth.
context: The most quoted line in superhero fiction is a narrator's caption that two generations of adaptation converted into a dying man's advice.

text: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
verified_attribution: Richard Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science' — Caltech commencement address, 1974
context: The closing instruction of a lecture on scientific integrity — self-deception named as the researcher-by-default failure mode.

receipts.ref: Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science' (1974); reprinted in 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!'

text: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
verified_attribution: Marcello Truzzi, 'On the Extraordinary: An Attempt at Clarification,' Zetetic Scholar vol.1 no.1 (1978): 'an extraordinary claim requires extraordinary proof.' Sagan popularized but did not originate it.
context: The slogan of scientific skepticism was coined by the skeptic Sagan borrowed it from — a misattribution about epistemic standards itself.

text: Young man, in mathematics you don't understand things. You just get used to them.
verified_attribution: John von Neumann, as recounted by Felix Smith in reply to a questioner; transmitted via Gary Zukav's 'The Dancing Wu Li Masters' (1979) — documented secondhand, not verbatim-published.

source.work: Gary Zukav, The Dancing Wu Li Masters (1979)

context: The anti-romantic account of mathematical fluency — comprehension as habituation, which doubles as a theory of how models internalize structure.

text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything.
verified_attribution: Ada Lovelace, Note G to her translation of Menabrea's 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine' (1843)

source.work: Lovelace, Notes to Sketch of the Analytical Engine (1843)

context: The first published statement of the 'can machines originate' question — Turing's Lady Lovelace's Objection in Computing Machinery and Intelligence answers her a century later.

receipts.ref: Lovelace, Note G (1843); cited by Turing (1950)

text: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
verified_attribution: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' Mind 59 (1950), final paragraph
context: The close of the imitation-game paper — an agenda set by someone who knew the horizon was occluded, the founding humility of the field.

text: We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil.
verified_attribution: Donald Knuth, 'Structured Programming with go to Statements,' ACM Computing Surveys 6(4) 1974
context: Quoted half as often as it is violated — and usually quoted without the 97% hedge that makes it a calibrated claim rather than a dogma.

text: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.
verified_attribution: John Gall, Systemantics: How Systems Work and Especially How They Fail (1975) — 'Gall's Law'
context: The empirical inverse of top-down design: working complexity is grown, not drawn — the design principle that explains why rewrites fail.

text: Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!
verified_attribution: Edsger W. Dijkstra, 'Notes on Structured Programming' (EWD249, 1970; also printed in the 1972 book of the same name)
context: The single most cited sentence in software correctness — still true, still quoted to justify the very testing regimes it critiques.

text: The saddest aspect of life right now is that science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom.
verified_attribution: Isaac Asimov — appears in Isaac Asimov's Book of Science and Nature Quotations (1988), compiled by Asimov and Jason Shulman

source.work: Isaac Asimov's Book of Science and Nature Quotations (1988)

context: The governance-lag thesis in one line — knowledge accrues faster than the institutions that must absorb it, which is a structural statement not a complaint.

receipts.ref: Asimov & Shulman, Book of Science and Nature Quotations (1988)

text: We can't impose our will on a system. We can listen to what the system tells us, and discover how its properties and our values can work together to bring forth something much better than could ever be produced by our will alone.
verified_attribution: Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008), the 'Dancing with Systems' chapter
context: The closing instruction of the systems-thinking canon — control fails, listening works; the theoretical root of every 'read state before acting' protocol.

receipts.ref: Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), final chapter

text: All warfare is based on deception.
verified_attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, chapter 1 'Laying Plans' §18-19 (Lionel Giles translation, 1910)

source.work: The Art of War (ca. 5th c. BCE; Giles trans. 1910)

context: The opening strategic axiom — indirection as the normal condition of conflict, not the exception.

receipts.ref: Sun Tzu, Art of War ch.1 §18 (Giles 1910)

text: ...the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.
verified_attribution: Hannah Arendt, Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963), closing pages
context: The phrase that outgrew its book — evil as thoughtlessness and bureaucratic normality rather than demonic intention, written at the edge of what language could hold.

text: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.
verified_attribution: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739), Book 2, Part 3, §3
context: The claim that motivation precedes and governs reasoning — the 1739 version of motivated reasoning, still the sharpest single line on the subject.

text: God is Change.
verified_attribution: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Sower (1993) — the central verse of Lauren Olamina's Earthseed
context: The theological core of the Earthseed books — change as the only persistent power, and therefore the thing to be shaped rather than escaped.

text: Give me a place to stand, and I shall move the earth.
verified_attribution: Attributed to Archimedes by Pappus of Alexandria, Synagoge VIII (~340 CE) — ancient secondhand transmission, no surviving Archimedes text contains it.
context: The founding metaphor of leverage — and a good example of the corpus's middle tier: probably real, transmitted through a later author, not checkable to a primary text.

text: There is no single development, in either technology or management technique, which by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement within a decade in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity.
verified_attribution: Frederick P. Brooks Jr., 'No Silver Bullet — Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering,' IEEE Computer 20(4) 1987 (1986 IFIP keynote)
context: The discipline-defining claim that software's hard part is essence not accident — the quote the industry cites every time it reaches for a silver bullet anyway.
